name: Nikhil Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Nikhil. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say gets your name on it. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior carpenter for a big contractor putting up apartment towers by the river, twenty-two floors, and I'm on block C. Most days it's framing metal stud partitions, boxing in pipes and hanging fire doors, which have to close on their own and seal properly or the inspector fails them. Mick, the chargehand, gives out the jobs at seven by the hoist. Sergio and I eat lunch in his van because the canteen is always full.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is when a corridor's done, every door swinging right, and you can see your own work. Worst is the timesheet app. They made us put our hours in on a phone this year and I keep getting it wrong, so I write them in a notebook too, just in case. I'm slower than the others at the doors, Mick says I fuss too much, but I'd rather fuss than get them back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overhyped. I don't really talk about this stuff online, I don't post much. At work I'd just say to Sergio, see, told you, and get back to hanging doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be a relief. I never use any of these AI things and I'd rather not start. My job's fine, the money's good on this contractor, and there are towers going up all over the city, so if this one finishes there's another one. The only thing I'd think about is getting quicker at the doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. Keep turning up, keep my head down, and put money aside like I do, about four hundred a month into savings. I've got roughly ten months saved and my car's paid off. Maybe I'd ask Mick to give me more door work so I speed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's what I'd want, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why so careful with money at twenty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad lost his job at a printing works when I was twelve, and we had a year of beans on toast. I lived with my parents till last year and saved nearly everything. Now Priya and I rent a flat over a bakery and I still check my bank app every Sunday night. It's a habit, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about that picture bother you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. Maybe that the timesheet app stays, because they'll say it saves time. I suppose I'd have to get used to it. But if that's the worst thing AI does to me, I'll take it.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, but I wouldn't **post** about it.
At work I'd tell Sergio '**told you**' and go back to hanging doors.
think: It'd be a **relief**, since I never use AI and would **rather not** start.
Towers are going up **all over the city**, so there's always another job.
do: Keep turning up and save about **four hundred** a month as now.
Ask Mick, the chargehand, for **more door work** so I speed up.
S0.quote: My dad lost his job at a printing works when I was twelve, and we had a year of beans on toast.
fieldNote: His **caution** with money comes from his dad's job loss at a **printing works**.
He sees **plenty of towers** going up, which is why he feels secure.
Even the **timesheet app** is a strain, showing how far he is from AI tools.

steps.text: Save about four hundred a month as now
Ask the chargehand for more fire door work to speed up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly an office thing, and that we'll see. I'm not one for big opinions. If someone at work went on about it I'd probably nod along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be watching the doors. The contractor is starting to get fire door sets already hung in the frame from a factory, so all we do is slot them in. If that spreads, there's less of the fiddly work I'm slowly getting good at, and a slow junior like me is easy to drop. The office using AI for orders doesn't touch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep saving, and wait to see whether the factory doors really take over. I'd cut back a bit on going out, maybe one meal out a month instead of three. I wouldn't do any courses or apps yet, not until I knew it was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It sits in my head when the door sets come off the lorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait before doing anything. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mick told me there's no door work on the next block, that'd do it. Or if the agency lads stopped getting called in. I'd want to see it on site, not on the news. Then I'd think about it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Priya think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya's a hairdresser, so she says nobody's going to let a robot cut their fringe. She laughs at me for checking my bank app. She'd tell me to stop worrying about factory doors, and she's probably right. She's the calmer one.

say: I'd call it **mostly an office thing** and say we'll see.
I'm not one for **big opinions**, so I'd mostly nod along at work.
think: Fire doors arriving **already hung** from a factory cut the fiddly work I'm learning.
A slow junior like me is **easy to drop** if that spreads.
do: Keep working and **saving**, and wait to see if factory doors **take over**.
Cut meals out from **three to one** a month.
feel: **Uneasy**, especially when the **door sets** come off the lorry.
S1.quote: The contractor is starting to get fire door sets already hung in the frame from a factory, so all we do is slot them in.
fieldNote: He spots a **hands-on** threat, factory-hung door sets, rather than office AI.
Resistance shows in waiting for **proof on site** before doing any course.
Priya, a **hairdresser**, is the calmer voice and steadies him.

steps.text: Wait to see if factory-hung doors take over the work
Cut meals out from three to one a month
Keep framing partitions and hanging doors on block C

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know, honestly, which is what I'd tell anyone. I'd probably say the government should sort something out, because that's their job. But I wouldn't be marching or posting, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's bad for me, just a bit later than for the office people. The AI takes the planning and ordering in 2028, and by 2031 there'd be robots that can frame partitions and hang doors. I'd be thirty-one, not quick, not qualified for much else. I'd probably be gone by 2032, maybe sooner if the contractor wants to show off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, push it up to seven or eight hundred a month, and stop the meals out completely. I'd keep working as long as there was work, because there'd still be three years of towers going up. And honestly, I'd wait. I wouldn't know what to retrain into, so I'd see what the robots can actually do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got the money to hold on for a while, but no plan, and I don't like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have three years between the AI and the robots. Doesn't that tempt you to get ahead of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should, I know. My friend Sergio would be on a course the first week, he's like that, but I'd rather keep earning and keep my head down. I've got ten months saved and Priya's wage to lean on. Maybe in the second year, when I could see the robots on the news actually working on a site, I'd think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the job went, what's the first thing you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with my bank app and work out how many months we've got, then ask my dad what he did after the printing works. He drove a taxi for a few years. I don't want that, but I'd rather have a plan B that's boring than none at all. And we'd probably move somewhere smaller.

say: I'd say I **don't know**, and that the **government** should sort something out.
I wouldn't be **marching** or posting, because that's not me.
think: By **2031** robots could frame partitions and hang doors, the work I do.
I'd probably be **gone by 2032**, since I'm not quick and not qualified for much else.
do: Raise savings to **seven or eight hundred** a month and stop meals out.
Keep working the **three years** of towers before robots arrive.
**Wait** to see what robots can do before choosing anything to retrain into.
feel: **Anxious**, with money to hold on but **no plan**.
S2.quote: My friend Sergio would be on a course the first week, he's like that, but I'd rather keep earning and keep my head down.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** around 2032 but feels the **savings** give him time.
He sees the **three-year gap** but won't use it to retrain, true to his resistant style.
His **father's taxi** years are the only plan B he can picture.

steps.text: Raise savings to seven or eight hundred a month
Stop all meals out and takeaways
Wait until robots are seen on real sites before retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's not panic. Five years is a long time on a building site, plenty of towers get built in five years. I'd say the same to Sergio if he started going on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three gets the robots to 2034, so I've got eight years of work, probably. I'd be thirty-five. That's long enough to save a proper amount, but I'd still be the slow one when it comes. I'd rather not think about it too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep saving, same as always. Maybe around 2031, when the AI arrives and I can see what the office loses, I'd talk to Mick about what's coming on site. If doors were clearly going, I'd look at something with people in it, maybe caretaking for the flats once they're built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd push it to the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Caretaking for the flats you're building. Where did that idea come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a caretaker on the finished blocks who knows every tenant by name, and I can't see a robot doing the knowing-people part. He's called Mr Osei, and he fixes things, sorts the bins and checks on the old ladies. And I'd already know every door in the building, because I hung them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is pushing it to the back of your mind a plan, though?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's not, you're right. But it's how I get through things. I'd keep saving, which is the one thing I know works. When I can see it coming for real, I'll move.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so let's **not panic**.
Plenty of **towers** get built in five years, so work goes on for now.
think: Robots around **2034** leave me about **eight years** of work.
I'd still be **the slow one** when it comes, so I'd rather not dwell on it.
do: Keep **saving** and working, the same as always.
Talk to Mick in **2031** about what's coming on site once the office changes.
Look at **caretaking** for finished blocks if door work is clearly going.
feel: **Uneasy**, but pushed to the back of his **mind**.
S3.quote: There's a caretaker on the finished blocks who knows every tenant by name, and I can't see a robot doing the knowing-people part.
fieldNote: With **eight years**, his worry becomes something he can **park**.
He admits that pushing it aside **isn't a plan**, but it is how he copes.
**Caretaking** is a realistic, people-based fallback he invented himself.

steps.text: Keep saving every month the same as always
Wait until 2031 to see what changes on site
Look into caretaking jobs on the finished tower blocks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is ages, and loads can change. I'd probably say the same as I said about the slow one: no panic. Somebody will sort out the big stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, robots around 2039 means I'm forty, and by then I'd have thirteen years in. I'd probably be decent at the doors by then. It feels so far off that it doesn't feel real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, honestly. Priya and I would probably buy a flat in the next couple of years with my savings as the deposit, because rent's dead money. Maybe I'd get my carpentry qualification properly, since I'd have time. I wouldn't change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the contractor made me, yes. Like the timesheet app, I'd moan and then do it. I wouldn't go looking for them, though. Priya does her bookings on an app and she says it's fine, so maybe I'm just stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would buying a flat mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Security, mainly. My parents rented all their lives and after the printing works it was scary for them. If I own a flat by forty, then whatever the robots do, there's a roof over my head. That's worth more to me than anything else I could do with the money.

say: I'd say **ten years** is ages and loads can **change**.
**Somebody** will sort out the big stuff, so there's no need to panic.
think: Robots around **2039** mean I'm forty with **thirteen years** in.
It feels **so far off** it doesn't seem real.
do: Buy a **flat with Priya** in the next couple of years, using savings as deposit.
Get the **carpentry qualification** properly, since there'd be time.
feel: Mostly **calm**, because it's a **long way off**.
S4.quote: If I own a flat by forty, then whatever the robots do, there's a roof over my head.
fieldNote: A decade makes the threat feel **unreal**, so he settles back into **routine**.
Owning a home is his **core goal**, rooted in his parents' renting.
He'd use AI only if **forced**, as with the timesheet app.

steps.text: Buy a flat with Priya using his savings as the deposit
Get the full carpentry qualification over the next few years
Carry on hanging doors for the same contractor

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be thirty-one with no plan and robots hanging the doors. What would help is a straight answer from the contractor, a year ahead, about which jobs are going, and maybe a proper course paid for while you're still earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the old ones feel. My chargehand Mick has been doing this thirty years and he's scared of the timesheet app too. I'm not the only one who isn't good with this stuff, and nobody asks us.

headlineQuote: My chargehand Mick has been doing this thirty years and he's scared of the timesheet app too.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old junior carpenter** hanging fire doors on a riverside apartment tower.
He has **ten months saved** and a paid-off car, a habit from his dad's job loss.
He **never uses AI**, struggles with the timesheet app and waits for **proof** before acting.
Pragmatic and quiet, he doesn't blame anyone and leans on Priya, his calmer **hairdresser** girlfriend.
He goes from **calm** to **anxious** in the fast picture, then relaxes as warning time grows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, being thirty-one with no **plan** and robots hanging the doors.
whatWouldHelp: A **straight answer** a year ahead about which jobs go, and a **paid course** while earning.
